source.text: שַׁלַּ֥ח לַחְמְךָ֖ עַל־פְּנֵ֣י הַמָּ֑יִם כִּֽי־בְרֹ֥ב הַיָּמִ֖ים תִּמְצָאֶֽנּוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Send your bread upon [the] face of the waters, for in [the] abundance of the days you will find it.

en.L: Send your bread on the face of the waters, \q for in [the] abundance of days you will find it.
en.B: Send your bread out on the surface of the waters, \q for after many days you will find it again.
en.R: Send your bread out across the water. \q After a long time it will come back to you.

decisions.choice: send your bread on the waters: let go of what you have and take a risk, trusting it to return
alternatives: trade by sea: send goods out on ships
be generous: give freely, and it will come back
decisions.reason: The saying is a picture, and readers differ on what it pictures. It may mean sending grain overseas in trade, which returns with profit after a long voyage (1 Kings 10:22). It may mean giving generously without counting the cost. Either way it urges bold action without knowing the outcome, which verses 2-6 go on to say.

decisions.choice: bread: grain, food, goods
decisions.reason: "Bread" can stand for grain or food in general (9:7).

decisions.choice: in the abundance of days: after a long time
decisions.reason: The return is not quick, but it comes.

decisions.choice: you will find it again (B); it will come back to you (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "again" or "come back", since what was sent away is found again.

source.text: תֶּן־חֵ֥לֶק לְשִׁבְעָ֖ה וְגַ֣ם לִשְׁמוֹנָ֑ה כִּ֚י לֹ֣א תֵדַ֔ע מַה־יִּהְיֶ֥ה רָעָ֖ה עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

records.literal_gloss: Give [a] portion to seven and even to eight, for not you know what will be disaster upon the earth.

en.L: Give a portion to seven, and also to eight, \q for you do not know what disaster will be on the earth.
en.B: Give a share to seven, and even to eight, \q for you do not know what disaster may come on the earth.
en.R: Give a share to seven, or even to eight. \q You do not know what disaster may strike the world.

decisions.choice: seven, and even eight: many, as many as you can
decisions.reason: A number followed by the next one is a Hebrew way of saying "many" or "more than enough" (Proverbs 30:15-31; Amos 1:3; Micah 5:4).

decisions.choice: a portion: a share given out
decisions.reason: The word (*cheleq*) here is a share that is handed out. As in verse 1, readers differ on whether the sense is spreading one's goods to reduce risk or giving generously to many, who may help in a bad time.

decisions.choice: disaster: misfortune
decisions.reason: The word (*ra'ah*) here is misfortune, not moral evil.

decisions.choice: a share
decisions.reason: Readable usually renders *cheleq* "what life gives you". Here it is a share handed out, so Readable says "a share", as Balanced does.

source.text: אִם־יִמָּלְא֨וּ הֶעָבִ֥ים גֶּ֨שֶׁם֙ עַל־הָאָ֣רֶץ יָרִ֔יקוּ וְאִם־יִפּ֥וֹל עֵ֛ץ בַּדָּר֖וֹם וְאִ֣ם בַּצָּפ֑וֹן מְק֛וֹם שֶׁיִּפּ֥וֹל הָעֵ֖ץ שָׁ֥ם יְהֽוּא׃

records.literal_gloss: If are filled the clouds [with] rain, upon the earth they empty [it]; and if falls [a] tree in the south or in the north, [the] place where falls the tree, there it will be.

en.L: If the clouds are filled with rain, they empty [it] on the earth; \q and if a tree falls in the south or in the north, \q [in the] place where the tree falls, there it will be.
en.B: When the clouds are full of rain, they pour it out on the earth; \q and whether a tree falls to the south or to the north, \q wherever the tree falls, there it will lie.
en.R: When clouds are full of rain, they pour it down on the earth. \q When a tree falls, whether to the south or to the north, \q it stays where it falls.

decisions.choice: the clouds and the tree: things happen as they will, beyond human control
decisions.reason: Rain falls when the clouds are full, and a fallen tree lies where it falls. People can neither cause such things nor change them. Verse 4 draws the lesson: do not wait for perfect conditions.

decisions.choice: there it will be: there it lies
decisions.reason: The verb form is unusual, close to Aramaic. It means "it will be" or "it stays".

source.text: שֹׁמֵ֥ר ר֖וּחַ לֹ֣א יִזְרָ֑ע וְרֹאֶ֥ה בֶעָבִ֖ים לֹ֥א יִקְצֽוֹר׃

records.literal_gloss: [One] watching [the] wind not will sow, and [one] looking at [the] clouds not will reap.

en.L: [One who] watches [the] wind will not sow, \q and [one who] looks at the clouds will not reap.
en.B: Whoever keeps watching the wind will never sow, \q and whoever keeps looking at the clouds will never reap.
en.R: If you wait for the wind to be just right, you will never plant. \q If you keep watching the clouds, you will never harvest.

decisions.choice: the wind and the clouds: weather that could spoil sowing or harvest
decisions.reason: Wind could blow seed away at sowing, and rain could spoil the grain at harvest (1 Samuel 12:17). A farmer who waits until there is no risk never sows or reaps.

decisions.choice: do not wait for perfect conditions
decisions.reason: No one can control the weather (verse 3) or know the future (verses 2, 5-6), so it is foolish to wait until everything is certain.

decisions.choice: keeps watching ... keeps looking (B); wait for the wind to be just right ... keep watching (R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew participles describe a habit. Balanced and Readable say "keep" to show this.

source.text: כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר אֵֽינְךָ֤ יוֹדֵ֨עַ֙ מַה־דֶּ֣רֶךְ הָר֔וּחַ כַּעֲצָמִ֖ים בְּבֶ֣טֶן הַמְּלֵאָ֑ה כָּ֗כָה לֹ֤א תֵדַע֙ אֶת־מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר יַעֲשֶׂ֖ה אֶת־הַכֹּֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: Just as not you know what [is the] way of the breath, to [the] bones in [the] womb of the pregnant [woman], so not you know the work of the God who makes the all.

en.L: Just as you do not know what [is] the way of the breath \q to the bones in the womb of the pregnant [woman], \q so you do not know the work of God, \q who makes everything.
en.B: Just as you do not know the path of the breath of life \q into the bones in a pregnant woman's womb, \q so you do not know the work of God, \q who makes all things.
en.R: You do not know how the breath of life comes \q into a baby's body as it grows inside its mother. \q In the same way, you cannot understand what God does. \q He is the one who makes everything.

decisions.choice: the breath: the breath of life that comes to an unborn child
decisions.reason: The word (*ruach*) means wind, breath or spirit. Verse 4 uses it for the wind. Here, with the bones in the womb, it most likely means the breath of life that God gives (12:7; Psalm 104:30). The two senses play against each other: no one knows the way of the wind, nor how life comes to a child.

decisions.choice: to the bones: into the bones of the child as it forms
alternatives: as the bones (grow): a second example, separate from the wind
decisions.reason: A small letter before "bones" can mean "to" or "like". Read as "to", the verse speaks of one mystery: how the breath of life enters the body in the womb. Read as "like", it gives two: the way of the wind, and the way bones grow in the womb.

decisions.choice: the bones in the womb: God's hidden work in forming a child
decisions.reason: Psalm 139:13-15 and Job 10:10-12 speak of God forming a person in the womb, where no one can see.

decisions.choice: you do not know the work of God, who makes everything
decisions.reason: God is the maker of all, and his work is beyond human knowing (3:11; 8:17).

decisions.choice: the breath of life
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say which breath is meant (m1).

decisions.choice: He is the one who
decisions.reason: Readable makes the last line a sentence of its own, with God as its subject.

source.text: בַּבֹּ֨קֶר֙ זְרַ֣ע אֶת־זַרְעֶ֔ךָ וְלָעֶ֖רֶב אַל־תַּנַּ֣ח יָדֶ֑ךָ כִּי֩ אֵֽינְךָ֨ יוֹדֵ֜עאֵ֣י זֶ֤ה יִכְשָׁר֙ הֲזֶ֣ה אוֹ־זֶ֔ה וְאִם־שְׁנֵיהֶ֥ם כְּאֶחָ֖ד טוֹבִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: In the morning sow your seed, and at evening do not let rest your hand; for not you know which will succeed, this or this, or whether both of them as one [are] good.

en.L: In the morning sow your seed, \q and at evening do not let your hand rest, \q for you do not know which will succeed, this or that, \q or whether both of them alike [will be] good.
en.B: Sow your seed in the morning, \q and in the evening do not let your hands be idle, \q for you do not know which will prosper, this or that, \q or whether both alike will turn out well.
en.R: Plant your seed in the morning, \q and keep working in the evening. \q You do not know which work will succeed, this or that. \q Maybe both will do well.

decisions.choice: morning and evening: early and late, all day long
alternatives: early in life and late in life
decisions.reason: Morning and evening together mean the whole day. Some read them also as the morning and evening of life, leading into verses 7-10.

decisions.choice: do not let your hand rest: keep working
decisions.reason: To let the hand rest is to stop work (7:18).

decisions.choice: you do not know which will succeed: work without knowing the outcome
decisions.reason: The chapter's advice: since no one can know which effort will succeed, do not hold back. Work hard and leave the outcome to God (verse 5).

decisions.choice: hands
decisions.reason: English speaks of idle hands in the plural.

source.text: וּמָת֖וֹק הָא֑וֹר וְט֥וֹב לַֽעֵינַ֖יִם לִרְא֥וֹת אֶת־הַשָּֽׁמֶשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: And sweet [is] the light, and good for the eyes to see the sun.

en.L: And sweet [is] the light, and [it is] good for the eyes to see the sun.
en.B: Light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun.
en.R: Light is sweet. It is good for your eyes to see the sun.

decisions.choice: light ... to see the sun: to be alive
decisions.reason: To see the light or the sun is to be alive (7:11; Job 3:16; Psalm 49:20). The verse begins the last section of Qoheleth's words (11:7-12:7): enjoy life while you are young, before age and death come.

decisions.choice: and: a new section begins
decisions.reason: The small word "and" links the section loosely to what comes before. The sayings in lines end with verse 6, and verses 7-10 are prose.

source.text: כִּ֣י אִם־שָׁנִ֥ים הַרְבֵּ֛ה יִחְיֶ֥ה הָאָדָ֖ם בְּכֻלָּ֣ם יִשְׂמָ֑ח וְיִזְכֹּר֙ אֶת־יְמֵ֣י הַחֹ֔שֶׁךְ כִּֽי־הַרְבֵּ֥ה יִהְי֖וּ כָּל־שֶׁבָּ֥א הָֽבֶל׃

records.literal_gloss: For if years many lives the human, in all of them let him rejoice, and let him remember the days of the darkness, for many they will be; all that comes [is] breath.

en.L: For if {{gender:a person|a man}} lives many years, let {{gender:them|him}} rejoice in all of them, and let {{gender:them|him}} remember the days of darkness, for they will be many; all that comes [is] breath.
en.B: However many years a person may live, let them enjoy them all, but let them remember that the days of darkness will be many. All that comes is a breath.
en.R: No matter how many years people live, they should enjoy every one of them. But they should remember that the dark days will be many. Everything that is coming will pass like a breath.

decisions.choice: the days of darkness: old age and death
decisions.reason: The days of darkness are set against the light of verse 7. They are the days of old age (12:1-2) and the long darkness of death (6:4; Job 10:21-22).

decisions.choice: breath: fleeting, soon gone
decisions.reason: *Hevel* (see 1:2). "All that comes" is everything still ahead; here the sense leans toward what is brief and passes.

decisions.choice: all that comes: everything still to come
decisions.reason: The words most likely mean whatever lies ahead. Some read: everyone who comes into the world.

decisions.choice: breath (L); a breath (B); will pass like a breath (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *hevel* keeps the picture of breath (see 1:2); Readable adds the sense (m2).

decisions.choice: let them enjoy ... let them remember (B); they should enjoy ... they should remember (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable speak of anyone, men and women; Literal keeps the singular with the gender setting.

source.text: שְׂמַ֧ח בָּח֣וּר בְּיַלְדוּתֶ֗יךָ וִֽיטִֽיבְךָ֤ לִבְּךָ֙ בִּימֵ֣י בְחוּרוֹתֶ֔ךָ וְהַלֵּךְ֙ בְּדַרְכֵ֣י לִבְּךָ֔ וּבְמַרְאֵ֖י עֵינֶ֑יךָ וְדָ֕ע כִּ֧י עַל־כָּל־אֵ֛לֶּה יְבִֽיאֲךָ֥ הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים בַּמִּשְׁפָּֽט׃

records.literal_gloss: Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let cheer you your heart in [the] days of your youth, and walk in [the] ways of your heart and in [the] sight of your eyes; and know that over all these will bring you the God into judgment.

en.L: Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart make you glad in the days of your youth, and go in the ways of your heart and in the sights of your eyes; and know that for all these God will bring you into judgment.
en.B: Be glad, young man, while you are young, and let your heart give you joy in the days of your youth. Follow the ways of your heart and what your eyes see, but know that God will call you to account for all these things.
en.R: Young man, be happy while you are young. Let your heart enjoy your youth. Do what your heart wants and what your eyes see. But remember that God will judge you for everything you do.

decisions.choice: walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes
decisions.reason: The law warns Israel not to follow their own heart and eyes (Numbers 15:39). Qoheleth tells the young to follow them, then adds that God will judge. Joy is God's gift (9:7), but it is lived before God.

decisions.choice: God will bring you into judgment: enjoyment is lived before God and answers to him
alternatives: God will judge whether you enjoyed his gifts
decisions.reason: The judgment is not a threat that cancels the call to joy; it sets the joy within limits. Some also read it the other way: God will hold people to account for refusing the joys he gave. The book ends on the same note (12:14).

decisions.choice: young man: one in the prime of youth
decisions.reason: The word (*bachur*) is a young man of fighting age. Qoheleth speaks to him as Proverbs speaks to "my son".

decisions.choice: call you to account
decisions.reason: Balanced says what being brought into judgment means; Literal keeps the Hebrew phrase.

decisions.choice: Do what your heart wants
alternatives: walk in the ways of your heart
decisions.reason: Readable says what the idiom means.

source.text: וְהָסֵ֥ר כַּ֨עַס֙ מִלִּבֶּ֔ךָ וְהַעֲבֵ֥ר רָעָ֖ה מִבְּשָׂרֶ֑ךָ כִּֽי־הַיַּלְד֥וּת וְהַֽשַּׁחֲר֖וּת הָֽבֶל׃

records.literal_gloss: And remove vexation from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh, for the youth and the dawn [are] breath.

en.L: And turn aside vexation from your heart, and make evil pass from your flesh, for youth and the dawn [of life are] breath.
en.B: So banish anxiety from your heart and put away pain from your body, for youth and the prime of life are a breath.
en.R: So do not let worry fill your heart, and do not let pain trouble your body. Youth and the best years of life soon pass, like a breath.

decisions.choice: vexation: anxiety, inner distress
decisions.reason: The word (*ka'as*) is the grief of 7:3 and the anger of 7:9. Here it is the worry and sorrow that spoil the joy of youth.

decisions.choice: evil: pain, harm, trouble of the body
decisions.reason: The word (*ra'ah*) here most likely means trouble or pain in the body, set beside trouble in the heart. Some take it as moral evil: put sin away from you.

decisions.choice: the dawn: the prime of life, perhaps the dark hair of youth
decisions.reason: The word appears only here. It may come from the word for dawn, the morning of life, or from the word for black, the dark hair of youth set against the white hair of age (12:5).

decisions.choice: breath: fleeting, soon gone
decisions.reason: *Hevel* (see 1:2). Youth does not last. The point is not that youth is worthless but that it passes, so it should be enjoyed.

decisions.choice: breath (L); a breath (B); soon pass, like a breath (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for *hevel* keeps the picture of breath (see 1:2); Readable adds the sense (m4).

decisions.choice: body
decisions.reason: "Flesh" here means the body.
